title: Laocoön. Equus in urbe
titleEn: Laocoön and the Horse Within the Walls — Aeneid II.195–286
source: P. Vergilius Maro, Aeneid, ed. J. B. Greenough, The Bucolics, Aeneid, and Georgics of Virgil (Boston: Ginn & Company, 1881), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0690.phi003.perseus-lat2, sha256 e639e6a0e27427ef. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Greenough's spelling kept (volnus, divom, Karthago, -is accusatives); his quotation marks printed as “ ”. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Sinon's speech is over, and Aeneas, still telling the story to Dido, says what it did: Sinon's lies and forced tears took the Trojans, whom ten years of war and a thousand ships had not beaten. Then a worse portent strikes them. Laocoön, chosen by lot as Neptune's priest, is sacrificing a bull at the altars when two huge serpents come over the calm sea from Tenedos, their blood-red crests rising above the waves. They slide past the terrified Trojans, seize Laocoön's two young sons and then the father as he runs to help, and wrap him in their coils; he strains at the knots, soaked in venom, and bellows like a wounded bull that has shaken off the axe. The snakes then slip away to the shrine of Pallas and hide under her feet and shield. The Trojans, seized by a new fear, conclude that Laocoön paid for wounding the sacred timber with his spear, and call for the image to be brought to the goddess's seat. They tear a gap in their own wall, set the horse on wheels and haul it in with ropes while boys and girls sing; four times it stalls on the threshold, and the weapons inside clash, yet they do not heed it. Cassandra, never believed, prophesies in vain, and the Trojans spend their last day hanging the shrines with garlands. At night, with the Trojans asleep, the Greek fleet returns from Tenedos at the flagship's signal, and Sinon opens the horse; the captains climb out and let their comrades in at the opened gates. Aeneas, asleep, sees Hector in a dream, torn and bleeding from his dragging, and speaks to him in sorrow and surprise.
part: Laocoön and the Horse Within the Walls (II.195–286)

sentences.t:
Talibus insidiis periurique arte Sinonis
credita res, captique dolis lacrimisque coactis,
quos neque Tydides, nec Larisaeus Achilles,
non anni domuere decem, non mille carinae.
sentences.l:
By such wiles and the art of perjured Sinon
the matter was believed, and we were caught by tricks and forced tears,
we whom neither Tydeus's son nor Larisaean Achilles,
not ten years, not a thousand ships had tamed.
sentences.i: By such treachery and the craft of perjured Sinon the tale won belief, and we were taken by trickery and by tears that were forced, we whom neither Diomedes nor Achilles of Larisa, nor ten years, nor a thousand ships had overcome.
sentences.n: Aeneas is still the speaker; Sinon's speech closed at line 194. 'Talibus insidiis… arte' — ablatives of means; 'credita res' means the story was believed, and 'captique (sumus)' leaves out the verb 'we were'. The relative 'quos' has no antecedent but the 'nos' we supply. 'Tydides' is Diomedes, son of Tydeus; 'Larisaeus' is a Thessalian epithet of Achilles (Larisa is a Thessalian city). 'domuere' = 'domuerunt' (the -ere ending; you'll see this constantly). The fourfold 'neque… nec… non… non' piles up what the Greeks could not do by force, so that the lie, not the war, took Troy.

sentences.t:
Hic aliud maius miseris multoque tremendum
obicitur magis, atque improvida pectora turbat.
sentences.l:
Here another thing, greater for the wretched and much more fearful,
is thrown before us, and troubles our unforeseeing hearts.
sentences.i: Then a second portent, greater and far more terrible, is thrust before us poor wretches and unsettles hearts that had no forewarning.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Hic' is 'at this point' in time. 'aliud maius… tremendum' — 'tremendum' is a gerundive used as an adjective, 'to be trembled at'; 'miseris' is a dative of the people it is set before. 'multoque… magis' — 'multo' is an ablative of degree of difference, 'much more'. 'obicitur' is a present tense in a past story (the historic present, which Aeneas uses often). 'improvida' is 'unforeseeing': the Trojans had no warning and no defence.

sentences.t:
Laocoön, ductus Neptuno sorte sacerdos,
sollemnis taurum ingentem mactabat ad aras.
sentences.l:
Laocoön, a priest chosen for Neptune by lot,
was sacrificing a huge bull at the customary altars.
sentences.i: Laocoön, drawn by lot as Neptune's priest, was slaughtering a huge bull at the solemn altars.
sentences.n: Greenough prints the diaeresis (Laocoön) to show the name has four syllables, La-o-co-on. 'ductus Neptuno sorte sacerdos' — 'ductus sorte' is 'drawn by lot'; 'Neptuno' is a dative of interest, 'for Neptune'. The sea god's priest is sacrificing when the serpents come out of the sea. 'sollemnis' means ritual, customary: the established rites. The imperfect 'mactabat' sets the scene before the sudden event.

sentences.i: And see: two serpents from Tenedos, over the quiet depths (the very telling of it makes me shudder), lie heavily on the sea in vast coils and make together for the shore;
sentences.n: 'Ecce autem' — 'behold, however': the sudden turn of the story. 'gemini… angues' — 'gemini' agrees with 'angues', separated from it by the parenthesis and the words before it in the next line. 'horresco referens' is the parenthesis between dashes: 'referens' is a present participle, 'as I tell it', Aeneas breaking off his own narration. 'a Tenedo' — the island where the Greek fleet hides (II.21–24). 'incumbunt pelago' — 'lie on, bear down on' takes the dative. The present tense runs from here.

sentences.t:
pectora quorum inter fluctus arrecta iubaeque
sanguineae superant undas;
sentences.l:
breasts of which amid the waves raised, and crests
blood-red, stand above the waves;
sentences.i: their breasts are reared up amid the billows, and their blood-red crests rise above the water;
sentences.n: 'quorum' is a connecting relative, 'of which (snakes)'. 'pectora… arrecta' — neuter plural participle of 'arrigo', 'raised upright'; 'iubae' are crests or manes, here the combs of the serpents, and 'sanguineae' agrees with it. 'superant' is 'overtop, rise above'. The picture is of two heads held high and the rest trailing.

sentences.t:
pars cetera pontum
pone legit, sinuatque immensa volumine terga.
sentences.l:
the other part the sea
behind skims, and curves the huge backs into a coil.
sentences.i: the rest of their length sweeps the sea behind them, and their huge backs curve in a coil.
sentences.n: 'pars cetera' is 'the remaining part' of each serpent; 'pone' is an adverb, 'behind'. 'legit' (from 'lego') means to pass along or skim over a surface, not 'read'. 'terga' is plural because there are two snakes, one back each. 'volumine' is an ablative of manner, 'in a coil'.

sentences.t: Fit sonitus spumante salo;
sentences.l: A sound is made, the salt water foaming;
sentences.i: A roar rises from the foaming brine;
sentences.n: 'Fit sonitus' — 'fio' is used as the passive of 'facio', 'a sound arises'. 'spumante salo' is an ablative absolute: 'salum' is the salt sea, 'spumante' agrees with it.

sentences.t:
iamque arva tenebant,
ardentisque oculos suffecti sanguine et igni,
sibila lambebant linguis vibrantibus ora.
sentences.l:
and now they were holding the fields,
and burning eyes, suffused with blood and fire,
hissing mouths they licked with quivering tongues.
sentences.i: and now they had gained the land; their burning eyes shot through with blood and fire, they licked their hissing mouths with flickering tongues.
sentences.n: 'arva tenebant' — 'were holding the fields' means they had reached land (the imperfect, as in the picture frozen at that moment). 'ardentis' = 'ardentes', accusative plural (the -is ending for -es; you'll see this constantly). 'suffecti' is the nominative plural participle of 'sufficio' (to suffuse, fill with colour) and agrees with 'angues'. 'ardentis oculos suffecti' — 'oculos' is an accusative of respect (a Greek-style accusative) with a passive participle: 'suffused as to their eyes'. 'sibila… ora' — 'sibila' is a neuter plural adjective, 'hissing', and the hyperbaton puts it and 'ora' on either side of 'linguis vibrantibus', as the tongues dart between.

sentences.t: Diffugimus visu exsangues:
sentences.l: We scatter at the sight, bloodless:
sentences.i: At the sight we scatter, drained of colour:
sentences.n: 'Diffugimus' — the prefix 'dis-' means we ran in different directions. 'visu' is the ablative of the fourth-declension noun 'visus', 'sight', of cause: 'at the sight'. 'exsangues' is 'bloodless', that is, white with fear. The colon announces what follows.

sentences.t:
illi agmine certo
Laocoönta petunt;
sentences.l:
they, in unswerving column,
Laocoön seek;
sentences.i: they, in an unswerving line, make for Laocoön;
sentences.n: 'illi' are the serpents. 'agmine certo' — an ablative of manner; 'agmen' is a marching column, and 'certo' is 'fixed, sure': they have a target. 'Laocoönta' is a Greek-style accusative in -a (a Greek name keeps its Greek ending).

sentences.i: and first each serpent clasps and winds about the small bodies of his two sons, and feeds with its bite upon the pitiful limbs;
sentences.n: 'parva duorum / corpora natorum' — 'duorum' and 'natorum' both qualify 'corpora' and are split by it: 'the small bodies of the two sons'. 'serpens… uterque' — 'uterque' means each of two, and takes a singular verb. 'amplexus' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'amplector' (a passive form with active sense), 'having embraced'. 'depascitur' is also deponent, 'feeds upon, devours'. 'miseros' is the adjective of pity, 'pitiful'.

sentences.t:
post ipsum auxilio subeuntem ac tela ferentem
corripiunt, spirisque ligant ingentibus;
sentences.l:
next himself, going up with aid and bearing weapons,
they seize, and with huge coils bind;
sentences.i: then the father himself, coming up to help with weapons in his hands, they seize and bind in their enormous coils;
sentences.n: 'post' is an adverb here, 'afterwards'. 'ipsum' is emphatic, 'the man himself'. 'auxilio' — 'to help', most naturally a dative of purpose; 'subeuntem' is 'coming up under' (the verb of approaching a danger). 'corripiunt' seizes in one grip, and 'spiris… ingentibus' is an ablative of means.

sentences.t:
et iam
bis medium amplexi, bis collo squamea circum
terga dati, superant capite et cervicibus altis.
sentences.l:
and now
twice the middle having clasped, twice about the neck scaly
backs having been put, they stand above with head and high necks.
sentences.i: and already, having twice clasped him about the waist, twice with their scaly backs laid round his throat, they tower above him with head and lofty neck.
sentences.n: 'medium' is used as a noun, 'his middle'; 'amplexi' is again the active-sense participle of the deponent (see above). 'collo… circum… dati' is 'circumdati' with the prefix pulled apart from the verb (tmesis, the cutting of a compound word), and 'collo' is the dative that 'circumdo' takes. 'squamea terga' — 'scaly backs', the accusative kept after the passive participle 'dati' (they have had their backs laid round). 'superant' is 'stand over, rise above': the snakes are higher than the man they bind.

sentences.t:
Ille simul manibus tendit divellere nodos,
perfusus sanie vittas atroque veneno,
clamores simul horrendos ad sidera tollit:
sentences.l:
He at once with hands strives to tear the knots apart,
smeared as to the fillets with gore and black venom,
at once horrible cries to the stars raises:
sentences.i: At the same moment he strains with his hands to wrench the coils away, his priestly bands drenched with gore and black venom, and at the same moment lifts a dreadful cry to the stars:
sentences.n: 'simul… simul' is 'at once… and at once', two things happening together. 'perfusus sanie vittas' — 'perfusus' is a passive participle 'drenched', and 'vittas' is an accusative of respect, 'drenched as to his fillets', a Greek-style construction that Virgil often uses with a passive participle (you'll see this constantly). The 'vittae' are the woollen bands a priest wears round the head. 'sanie' (gore) and 'atro veneno' (black venom) are ablatives of means. 'tendit divellere' — 'tendo' with an infinitive is the poetic 'strains to'.

sentences.t:
quales mugitus, fugit cum saucius aram
taurus, et incertam excussit cervice securim.
sentences.l:
such bellowings as, when wounded, flees the altar
the bull, and has shaken from the neck the ill-aimed axe.
sentences.i: such a bellowing as a wounded bull makes when he flees the altar, having shaken the ill-aimed axe from his neck.
sentences.n: The simile makes Laocoön's cry the cry of his own sacrificial bull; compare the bull-at-the-altar simile Homer uses for a dying man in the Iliad (book 20). 'quales mugitus' is an accusative standing in apposition to 'clamores', 'such bellowings'. 'incertam… securim' — the axe whose blow was 'uncertain', that is, did not do its work; 'cervice' is an ablative of separation. The picture echoes Laocoön's own sacrifice at 201–202: the priest ends like a victim.

sentences.t:
At gemini lapsu delubra ad summa dracones
effugiunt saevaeque petunt Tritonidis arcem,
sub pedibusque deae clipeique sub orbe teguntur.
sentences.l:
But the twin, with a glide, to the topmost shrines, the dragons
escape, and the fierce Tritonian's citadel seek,
and beneath the goddess's feet and beneath the shield's round are covered.
sentences.i: But the two serpents glide off to the highest shrine, make for the citadel of the fierce Tritonian goddess, and hide beneath her feet and under the round of her shield.
sentences.n: 'dracones' is another word for the same serpents, as the story shifts to what they do after the deed. 'lapsu' — an ablative of manner, 'in a glide'; 'delubra ad summa' — the preposition is placed between its noun and adjective. 'Tritonidis' is Pallas Athena (Minerva), the Tritonian: the name probably goes back to a lake or river Triton; 'saevae' (agreeing with it) calls her fierce. 'clipei… orbe' — the circle of the shield. 'teguntur' is passive in form but reflexive in sense. They go to the goddess to whom, in Sinon's tale, the horse is offered, and the Trojans read this as a verdict.

sentences.t:
Tum vero tremefacta novus per pectora cunctis
insinuat pavor, et scelus expendisse merentem
Laocoönta ferunt, sacrum qui cuspide robur
laeserit, et tergo sceleratam intorserit hastam.
sentences.l:
Then truly through trembling breasts, for all, a new
creeps in fear, and that the crime has paid, deserving it,
Laocoön, they say, who the sacred oak with spear
has wounded, and on its back hurled the accursed lance.
sentences.i: Then indeed a new fear creeps through every shaken heart, and they say that Laocoön has paid for his crime, and deserved to, for he wounded the sacred timber with his spear and hurled his guilty lance at its back.
sentences.n: 'tremefacta… pectora' is a neuter plural participle agreeing with 'pectora', 'made to tremble'; 'cunctis' is a dative of interest, 'for all'. 'insinuat' is 'winds itself in'. 'scelus expendisse merentem Laocoönta ferunt' — an accusative and infinitive after 'ferunt', 'they say that Laocoön has paid (expendisse) the penalty of his crime, deserving it (merentem)'. 'qui… laeserit… intorserit' — the perfect subjunctives give the Trojans' reasoning ('because he had…'), not Virgil's own statement. 'sacrum… robur' calls the wood of the horse consecrated; 'tergo' is 'at its back', and the weapon is 'sceleratam', accursed. The Trojans read the omen exactly wrong.

sentences.t:
Ducendum ad sedes simulacrum orandaque divae
numina conclamant.
sentences.l:
To be led to its seat, the image, and to be entreated, the goddess's
divinity, they cry out together.
sentences.i: They cry out together that the image must be led to its seat and the goddess's power entreated.
sentences.n: 'Ducendum… simulacrum orandaque… numina' — gerundives with 'esse' left out, 'must be led, must be entreated', in an indirect statement after 'conclamant' ('simulacrum' and 'numina' are the accusative subjects). Line 233 is a half-line, one of Virgil's unfinished lines. 'simulacrum' is the horse, called an image as Sinon called it 'effigies' (accusative 'effigiem', line 184). 'ad sedes' is 'to its seat', the goddess's temple on the citadel; 'divae numina' is 'the goddess's divinity' (the plural 'numina' is used here for a single deity). 'conclamant' — the 'con-' says they all shout together.

sentences.t: Dividimus muros et moenia pandimus urbis.
sentences.l: We divide the walls and open up the city's ramparts.
sentences.i: We break apart the walls and lay open the city's defences.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Dividimus' — 'we part, cut through': Aeneas says 'we' and includes himself in the mistake. 'moenia pandimus' — 'moenia' are the ramparts, and 'pandimus' is 'we open wide'. The Trojans make the hole in their own wall to bring the horse in.

sentences.t:
Accingunt omnes operi, pedibusque rotarum
subiciunt lapsus, et stuppea vincula collo
intendunt:
sentences.l:
All gird themselves for the work, and under its feet, of wheels
they set glidings, and hempen bonds on its neck
stretch:
sentences.i: All gird themselves for the work; they set gliding wheels under its feet and stretch ropes of hemp about its neck:
sentences.n: 'Accingunt omnes operi' — 'accingo' is to gird, here reflexive in sense ('everyone braces himself'), and 'operi' is a dative of purpose. 'pedibus… subiciunt' — 'they place under the feet' of the horse. 'rotarum lapsus' is 'the glidings of wheels', that is, gliding wheels (the genitive does the work of an adjective). 'stuppea vincula' are bonds of tow or hemp; 'collo' is a dative, and 'intendunt' is 'stretch tight'. The colon opens the hauling.

sentences.t:
scandit fatalis machina muros,
feta armis.
sentences.l:
climbs, the fateful engine, the walls,
pregnant with arms.
sentences.i: the engine of fate climbs the walls, heavy with armed men.
sentences.n: 'machina' is the horse, now a siege-engine and a bringer of fate. 'fatalis' (nominative singular) means doomed or fate-laden. 'feta armis' — 'feta' is 'pregnant, teeming', the birth image Virgil keeps using of the horse (see 'utero' at 243 and 258); 'armis' is an ablative with it. 'scandit' — 'climbs', as an engine going up a ramp.

sentences.t:
Pueri circum innuptaeque puellae
sacra canunt, funemque manu contingere gaudent.
sentences.l:
Boys round about and unwedded girls
sing holy songs, and to touch the rope with the hand rejoice.
sentences.i: Boys and unmarried girls around it sing sacred songs and are glad to lay a hand upon the rope.
sentences.n: 'sacra canunt' — 'sacra' (neuter plural) are 'holy things', that is hymns or sacred songs. 'innuptae' means unmarried, 'not yet wed'; the contrast with what is coming is plain. 'contingere gaudent' — 'gaudeo' takes an infinitive in poetry, 'are glad to touch'. 'funem' is the rope by which the horse is hauled.

sentences.t: Illa subit, mediaeque minans inlabitur urbi.
sentences.l: It goes up, and threatening glides into the midst of the city.
sentences.i: It moves forward and slips, menacing, into the heart of the city.
sentences.n: 'Illa' is the horse. 'subit' is 'comes up, advances'. 'mediae… urbi' — a dative with the compound verb 'inlabitur' (Greenough's spelling; the familiar 'illabitur'), 'glides into the midst of the city'. 'minans' is a present participle, 'threatening', the word that undoes the festive picture just before it.

sentences.t:
O patria, O divom domus Ilium, et incluta bello
moenia Dardanidum, quater ipso in limine portae
substitit, atque utero sonitum quater arma dedere:
sentences.l:
O fatherland, O house of the gods, Ilium, and famed in war
walls of the Dardanids, four times in the very threshold of the gate
it halted, and from the womb a sound four times the arms gave:
sentences.i: O my country! O Ilium, home of the gods, and you walls of the Dardanians, famous in war! Four times on the very threshold of the gate it stopped, and four times the weapons in its belly rang out:
sentences.n: An apostrophe: Aeneas turns from narrating to calling on his lost city. 'divom domus' — 'divom' is the old genitive plural for 'divorum'; both nouns are in the vocative, with 'Ilium' (neuter) in apposition. 'Dardanidum' is the genitive plural of the patronymic, 'the Dardanids', the descendants of Dardanus, i.e. the Trojans; 'moenia' is a vocative too. 'quater' — four times, an ill omen. 'substitit' is the horse's check at the threshold; 'utero' is the womb again; 'dedere' = 'dederunt'. The Trojans hear the weapons and go on.

sentences.t:
instamus tamen inmemores caecique furore,
et monstrum infelix sacrata sistimus arce.
sentences.l:
we press on nonetheless, unmindful and blind with frenzy,
and the ill-starred monster we set in the consecrated citadel.
sentences.i: Yet we press on, heedless, blinded by madness, and set the baleful monster in the sacred citadel.
sentences.n: 'inmemores' is Greenough's spelling (the familiar form is 'immemores'), 'unmindful' of the warning. 'caeci furore' — 'caeci' is 'blind', with 'furore' an ablative of cause, 'with frenzy'. 'monstrum infelix' — 'monstrum' is a portent or marvel, 'infelix' ill-omened, unlucky. 'sistimus' is 'we set up, station'. 'sacrata arce' is the citadel consecrated to the gods, polluted by what is set in it.

sentences.t:
Tunc etiam fatis aperit Cassandra futuris
ora, dei iussu non umquam credita Teucris.
sentences.l:
Then even for fates to come opens
her mouth Cassandra, by the god's command never believed by the Teucrians.
sentences.i: Even then Cassandra opens her lips to the fates to come, by the god's decree never believed by the Trojans.
sentences.n: 'Cassandra' is Priam's daughter, to whom Apollo gave prophecy and then, when she refused him, the curse that no one would believe her. 'dei iussu' — 'by the command of the god', an ablative of cause: the god is Apollo, though the text does not name him. 'fatis… futuris' — 'fatis' is a dative of interest: she 'opens her mouth for' (to proclaim) the fates to come. 'non umquam' is 'never at any time'. 'Teucris' — the Trojans, named from Teucer, an early king of Troy; here a dative of agent after the participle 'credita'.

sentences.t:
Nos delubra deum miseri, quibus ultimus esset
ille dies, festa velamus fronde per urbem.
sentences.l:
We, the shrines of the gods, wretched, for whom the last
that day was to be, with festal leafage veil through the city.
sentences.i: And we, poor wretches, for whom that day was to be the last, hang festive garlands on the shrines of the gods all through the city.
sentences.n: 'Nos… miseri' — the wretched 'we' stands first, and the sentence ends in bitter irony. 'quibus ultimus esset ille dies' — a relative clause with the subjunctive, which marks the narrator's hindsight: 'for whom that day was (to be) the last'. 'deum' = 'deorum' (the old genitive plural contraction). 'velamus fronde' — 'veil with leafy boughs', hanging the shrines with garlands. 'festa' is 'festal'.

sentences.i: Meanwhile the heavens wheel, and night rushes up from the ocean, wrapping earth and sky, and the Myrmidons' guile, in its vast shadow;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Vertitur' is passive in form with middle sense, 'turns itself, wheels'. 'oceano' — an ablative of separation, as the night comes up out of the Ocean at the world's edge. 'involvens' is a present participle; 'umbra magna' is the ablative of means. 'polum' is the pole, so the sky. 'Myrmidonum' (the old genitive plural) are Achilles' men from Thessaly, here put for the Greeks. The shadow covers the Greeks' trick as well as the world.

sentences.t:
fusi per moenia Teucri
conticuere, sopor fessos complectitur artus:
sentences.l:
stretched out along the walls, the Teucrians
are silent, sleep embraces their weary limbs:
sentences.i: the Trojans lie sprawled and silent about the walls, and sleep enfolds their weary limbs:
sentences.n: 'fusi' is the participle of 'fundo' (to pour), 'poured out, sprawled'. 'conticuere' = 'conticuerunt' and echoes the very first word of the book (line 1), the silence of the hall now become the silence of the city. 'fessos artus' are 'tired limbs'. The colon prepares for what the silence allows.

sentences.t:
et iam Argiva phalanx instructis navibus ibat
a Tenedo tacitae per amica silentia lunae
litora nota petens,
sentences.i: and already the Argive host, in ships drawn up in ranks, was sailing from Tenedos, in the kindly hush of the silent moon, making for the shores they knew,
sentences.n: 'phalanx' is a Greek word for a battle-line, here the whole host. 'instructis navibus' — an ablative of attendant circumstance, 'with ships ordered in line'. 'a Tenedo' — the island where the fleet hid (see 203). 'tacitae per amica silentia lunae': the moon is silent, and the hush is 'friendly' because it favours the Greeks' plot. 'litora nota petens' — 'petens' agrees with 'phalanx', the Troad shores that the Greeks already know. The sentence is long and runs on.

sentences.t:
flammas cum regia puppis
extulerat, fatisque deum defensus iniquis
inclusos utero Danaos et pinea furtim
laxat claustra Sinon.
sentences.l:
flames when the royal ship
had raised, and by the gods' unjust fates protected,
the Danaans shut in the womb and the pine
bolts secretly looses Sinon.
sentences.i: once the flagship had held up its signal fire; and Sinon, shielded by the gods' unkind fates, stealthily looses the pine bars that hold the Danaans shut in the horse's womb.
sentences.n: 'flammas cum regia puppis extulerat' — 'cum' with the pluperfect indicative gives the signal, 'when the flagship had raised its flames'; 'regia puppis' is the royal ship (Agamemnon's). 'fatis deum defensus iniquis' — 'deum' is 'deorum'; 'fatis… iniquis' is an ablative of means and cause, 'protected by the unjust fates' (unjust to Troy). 'utero' is the womb again. 'pinea claustra' are bars of pine, 'laxat' loosens, 'furtim' means by stealth. The hinge of the night: the man we saw weeping is the one who opens the horse.

sentences.t:
Illos patefactus ad auras
reddit equus,
sentences.l:
Them, opened to the air,
gives back the horse,
sentences.i: The horse, thrown open, gives them back to the open air,
sentences.n: 'Illos' are the Danaans of the last unit. 'patefactus' (participle of 'patefacio') agrees with 'equus', 'having been opened'. 'reddit' is 'gives back, returns', as a thing deposited. 'ad auras' is 'to the breezes', the open air. The comma carries the sentence on to the list of leaders.

sentences.t:
laetique cavo se robore promunt
Thessandrus Sthenelusque duces, et dirus Ulixes,
demissum lapsi per funem, Acamasque, Thoasque,
Pelidesque Neoptolemus, primusque Machaon,
et Menelaus, et ipse doli fabricator Epeos.
sentences.l:
and joyful, from the hollow oak they bring themselves forth
Thessandrus and Sthenelus, the leaders, and dire Ulysses,
having slid down a lowered rope, and Acamas, and Thoas,
and Pelides Neoptolemus, and first Machaon,
and Menelaus, and Epeos himself, the maker of the trick.
sentences.i: and glad to be out, they come forth from the hollow timber, sliding down a lowered rope: Thessandrus and Sthenelus, the captains, grim Ulysses, Acamas and Thoas, Achilles' son Neoptolemus, Machaon first of all, Menelaus, and Epeos himself, who contrived the trick.
sentences.n: A roll-call of the men in the horse. 'se… promunt' — 'they bring themselves forth'; 'laeti', glad at being out. 'cavo… robore' is the hollow oak (the oak again, for fir or pine elsewhere). 'demissum lapsi per funem' — 'lapsi' is the participle of 'labor', 'having slid', with 'demissum funem' (a rope let down) as the way they came. 'Pelides Neoptolemus' — 'Pelides' is the patronymic from Peleus, normally Achilles, here his grandson; Neoptolemus (also named Pyrrhus) figures largely later in the book. 'primusque Machaon' — Machaon, the physician, is 'first' out, or foremost. 'ipse doli fabricator' — Epeos, the builder, who made the horse in the Greek tradition; 'doli' is a genitive of the thing made, 'fabricator of the trick'.

sentences.t: Invadunt urbem somno vinoque sepultam;
sentences.l: They invade the city buried in sleep and wine;
sentences.i: They fall upon a city sunk deep in sleep and wine;
sentences.n: 'Invadunt' is 'they go in upon', an attack. 'sepultam' is 'buried' (the participle of 'sepelio', the verb for burying the dead), and 'somno vinoque' are ablatives of means. The city is drunk as well as asleep; the metaphor of burial is Virgil's.

sentences.t:
caeduntur vigiles, portisque patentibus omnis
accipiunt socios atque agmina conscia iungunt.
sentences.l:
the watchmen are cut down, and, the gates open, all
they receive their comrades, and join the accomplice columns.
sentences.i: The watchmen are cut down; the gates stand open and they take in all their comrades, and join to their own the ranks that shared the plot.
sentences.n: 'caeduntur vigiles' — the passive of 'caedo', cut down, the sentries. 'portisque patentibus' is an ablative absolute, 'the gates standing open'. 'omnis' = 'omnes', accusative plural, going with 'socios' (hyperbaton, 'all the comrades'). 'agmina conscia' — 'conscia' means 'sharing the knowledge' (conscious with), the ranks who were in the plot; the Greeks outside and the Greeks inside make one army.

sentences.t:
Tempus erat, quo prima quies mortalibus aegris
incipit, et dono divom gratissima serpit.
sentences.l:
It was the time when the first rest for weary mortals
begins, and by the gift of the gods most welcome creeps in.
sentences.i: It was the hour when first sleep begins for weary mortals, and steals over them, a most welcome gift of heaven.
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and the dream begins. 'Tempus erat, quo' — 'quo' is the relative adverb 'when', so 'it was the time at which'. 'quies' is rest, i.e. sleep. 'aegris' means worn out, sick with toil. 'dono divom' — 'divom' is 'divorum' (the old genitive plural again), and 'dono' an ablative: it comes as a gift of the gods. 'serpit' is 'creeps', in a book whose last scenes were serpents.

sentences.t:
In somnis, ecce, ante oculos maestissimus Hector
visus adesse mihi, largosque effundere fletus,
raptatus bigis, ut quondam, aterque cruento
pulvere, perque pedes traiectus lora tumentis.
sentences.l:
In dreams, behold, before my eyes most sorrowful Hector
seemed to be present to me, and copious tears to pour out,
dragged by a chariot-pair, as once, and black with gory
dust, and through the feet, swollen, pierced with thongs.
sentences.i: In my sleep, and look, before my eyes Hector, in deepest sorrow, seemed to stand beside me and pour out floods of tears, torn along by the chariot as he once was, black with bloody dust, and with thongs run through his swollen feet.
sentences.n: 'visus adesse mihi' — 'videor' (passive of 'video') means 'I seem', here 'he seemed to be there for me'. Hector, killed by Achilles, was dragged round Troy behind his chariot (Iliad 22); a dead man comes in a dream, as Patroclus appears to Achilles (Iliad 23). 'raptatus bigis' — 'raptatus' is a participle of the frequentative 'rapto', dragged again and again; 'bigis' is the two-horse chariot, in the ablative of means. 'aterque cruento pulvere' — 'black with bloody dust', ablative of respect. 'perque pedes traiectus lora' — 'traiectus' (pierced through) with 'lora' as a retained accusative: 'having had the thongs passed through' his feet, the thongs that tied him to the chariot. 'tumentis' = 'tumentes', accusative plural, agreeing with 'pedes'.

sentences.t:
Ei mihi, qualis erat, quantum mutatus ab illo
Hectore, qui redit exuvias indutus Achilli,
vel Danaum Phrygios iaculatus puppibus ignis,
sentences.l:
Ah me, what a one he was, how much changed from that
Hector who returns, clad in the spoils of Achilles,
or who hurled Phrygian fires at the Danaans' ships,
sentences.i: Alas, what a sight he was, how changed from that Hector who came back wearing the spoils of Achilles, or who hurled Phrygian fire at the Greek ships,
sentences.n: 'Ei mihi' — a cry of grief, 'ah me'. 'qualis erat, quantum mutatus' — exclamatory clauses, 'what a one he was', 'how much changed'. 'ab illo Hectore, qui redit…' — the old Hector is the one who 'returns' (historic present) in the spoils of Achilles, which he took from Patroclus's body (Iliad 17), or who hurled fire at the Greek ships (Iliad 15–16). 'exuvias indutus' — 'indutus' is a participle in the middle sense, 'having put on', with an accusative object, the Greek-style construction again (as with 'vittas' at 221). 'Achilli' is an old genitive of Achilles. 'Danaum' is the old genitive plural of 'Danai', and 'puppibus' a dative, 'at the ships'. 'ignis' = 'ignes'. 'vel' here is 'or'.

sentences.t:
squalentem barbam et concretos sanguine crinis
volneraque illa gerens, quae circum plurima muros
accepit patrios.
sentences.l:
a squalid beard and hair matted with blood
bearing, and those wounds, which around very many the walls
he received, his fatherland's.
sentences.i: bearing a filthy beard, and hair clotted with blood, and all those wounds he took, so many of them, round his city's walls.
sentences.n: 'gerens' belongs to Hector: 'bearing, carrying', as if the beard, the hair and the wounds were what he carried with him. 'squalentem' is 'rough, encrusted'; 'concretos sanguine' — 'concretos' means matted or clotted, with 'sanguine' as an ablative, and 'crinis' = 'crines'. 'volnera' is Greenough's spelling of 'vulnera'. 'quae circum plurima muros / accepit patrios' — 'circum' is separated from its noun 'muros' by 'plurima', 'very many'; 'patrios' is 'his fatherland's, his father's', the walls of Troy.

sentences.t:
Ultro flens ipse videbar
Compellare virum et maestas expromere voces:
sentences.l:
Of my own accord, weeping, I myself seemed
to address the man and utter sad words:
sentences.i: I myself, weeping, seemed unbidden to speak to him and bring out words of sorrow:
sentences.n: 'Ultro' is 'of my own accord, unprompted': the ghost has not spoken, and Aeneas speaks first. 'videbar' is 'I seemed' (the passive of 'video' again, as at 271). 'compellare' means 'to address' and 'expromere' to bring out; the two infinitives depend on 'videbar'. 'virum' — 'the man', Hector. The colon opens Greenough's speech mark in the next unit.

sentences.t:
“O lux Dardaniae, spes O fidissima Teucrum,
quae tantae tenuere morae?
sentences.l:
“O light of Dardania, O hope most faithful of the Teucrians,
what such great delays have held you?
sentences.i: “O light of Dardania, O surest hope of the Trojans, what long delays have kept you from us?
sentences.n: The speech mark is Greenough's: Aeneas speaks to the dream-figure of Hector; the speech ends at the last line of this part. 'spes O fidissima' — the 'O' in the middle of the phrase is a Virgilian habit; 'fidissima' is a superlative, 'most trustworthy'. 'Dardaniae' is Troy's land, from Dardanus. 'quae tantae tenuere morae' — 'te' is left out ('what so great delays held you?'); 'tenuere' = 'tenuerunt'. The question piles up reproaches in the form of questions.

sentences.t:
Quibus Hector ab oris
exspectate venis?
sentences.l:
From what shores, Hector,
long awaited, do you come?
sentences.i: From what shores do you come, Hector, so long awaited?
sentences.n: 'Quibus… ab oris' — the preposition is set between 'quibus' and 'oris'. 'exspectate' is a vocative participle, 'you who were waited for', a long-awaited arrival. The name Hector is put at the middle of the question. Aeneas, in his dream, greets him as if he had only been delayed.

sentences.t:
Ut te post multa tuorum
funera, post varios hominumque urbisque labores
defessi aspicimus!
sentences.l:
How, after many deaths of your own,
after various toils of men and the city,
wearied, we look upon you!
sentences.i: How we look on you now, worn out as we are, after so many deaths among your own, after all the manifold sufferings of men and city!
sentences.n: 'Ut' with the indicative is exclamatory, 'how!'. 'post multa tuorum / funera' — 'tuorum' is a substantive, 'your people', so 'after the many deaths of your own'. 'varios hominumque urbisque labores' — 'labores' are toils or sufferings, and 'hominum urbisque' joins the people and the city, the genitives saying whose toils they were. 'defessi' is 'worn out' and nominative plural with 'aspicimus'. The sentence is a greeting with the grief mixed into it.

sentences.t:
Quae causa indigna serenos
foedavit voltus?
sentences.l:
What undeserved cause has defiled
your serene features?
sentences.i: What unworthy cause has marred that calm face of yours?
sentences.n: 'Quae causa indigna' — 'indigna' is 'undeserved, unworthy'. 'serenos voltus' — 'serenos' is 'calm, clear' (the opposite of what we have just seen); 'voltus' is Greenough's spelling of 'vultus', a plural of the one face. 'foedavit' is 'has defiled, disfigured', from 'foedus' (foul). Aeneas sees the ruin of the face and does not understand.

sentences.t: Aut cur haec volnera cerno?”
sentences.l: Or why do I see these wounds?”
sentences.i: Or why do I see these wounds on you?”
sentences.n: The closing mark is Greenough's: Aeneas's address to Hector ends here, and the ghost's answer follows. 'Aut cur' — 'aut' adds an alternative question, 'or why?'. 'haec volnera' — 'volnera' is Greenough's spelling of 'vulnera', the wounds that have just been described (277–279).
